steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our computer vision paper on pose-invariant object recognition and retrieval. The idea is to learn separate category-based and object-identity-based embeddings instead of one shared space; cover the motivation, what prior multi-view methods miss, our encoder and training losses, and the main gains we get.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Pose-invariant recognition and retrieval: the problem and why it matters
- Main claim: disentangle category-based and object-identity-based learning
- Illustration (Fig. 1): chairs vs. stools
- Prior work: multi-view networks and pose-invariant embeddings, and where they fall short
- Our key difference: two distinct embedding spaces, and the resulting improvements
- The encoder: Pose-invariant Attention Network (PAN)
- Training: two pose-invariant losses

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem
  - pose-invariant recognition and retrieval; important in computer vision
  - applications: robotic automation, automatic checkout, inventory management
  - same-category objects look very different from different viewpoints; humans still recognize them from arbitrary viewpoints
  - goal: map images to embeddings; same-category embeddings pulled together across all viewpoints, relative to other categories
- Main claim
  - performance of pose-invariant learning significantly improved by disentangling category-based learning from object-identity-based learning
- Fig. 1 example
  - database with different chairs and different stools
  - category embeddings for chair class and stool class -> capture what discriminates them: presence/absence of a back-rest
  - object-identity embeddings -> what is distinctive about each object type vs. others in the same category
  - e.g. lounge chairs vs. desk chairs
- Prior work
  - multi-view deep networks -> aggregated multi-view representations, variability under pose transformations
  - good on category-level tasks with multiple views at inference; degrade with a single view
  - real-world apps often need single-view inference
  - Ho et al.: family of pose-invariant embeddings; single-view embeddings clustered around multi-view embedding, which clusters around a category proxy
  - weakness: does not separate two different objects of the same category (two chairs, two kettles)
  - so prior approaches good at category-level, not object-level tasks (Tables 2, 3)
- Our difference
  - learn category-specific and object-specific features simultaneously in two distinct embedding spaces (lower panel of Fig. 1)
  - category space: same-category objects close, shared characteristics
  - object-identity space: object types as separated as their differentiating attributes dictate
  - more discriminative overall; better recognition and retrieval, esp. single-view query
  - single-view recognition accuracy gains: 20.0% ModelNet40, 46.5% FG3D, 2.0% ObjectPI
  - single-view retrieval mAP gains: 33.7% ModelNet-40, 56.9% FG3D, 18.8% ObjectPI
- PAN encoder
  - Pose-invariant Attention Network
  - shared CNN backbone: visual features common to both representations, from images of an object at different viewpoints
  - two fully connected layers -> separate low-dim category and object-identity embeddings
  - self-attention aggregates features across views -> multi-view embeddings
  - dual embeddings defined in Section 3; category and object-level recognition and retrieval, single and multiple views
- Losses
  - pose-invariant category loss + pose-invariant object-identity loss, jointly optimized
  - category loss: cluster instances of different objects of the same category, separate different categories (category space)
  - object-identity loss: cluster instances with same object-identity label; separate confusing instances with different identity labels from the same category (object space)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Pose-invariant recognition and retrieval is an important problem in computer vision, and it has practical applications like robotic automation, automatic checkout systems, and inventory management. Many objects that belong to the same general category can look very different from different viewpoints, but humans have no difficulty recognizing them from any viewpoint. In pose-invariant recognition and retrieval the focus is on mapping object images to embedding vectors so that the embeddings of objects in the same category are pulled together for all the viewpoints we have, relative to the embeddings of objects from different categories.

Our work shows that the performance of this kind of pose-invariant learning can be improved significantly if the category-based learning is disentangled from the object-identity-based learning.

Fig. 1 shows what we mean by disentangling the category-based representation from the object-identity-based representation. Say an object database has images of different types of chairs and different types of stools. We want the network to learn category-based embedding vectors for the chair class and for the stool class. These embeddings need to capture what discriminates the chairs from the stools the most, which is whether there is a back-rest or not. At the same time we also want the network to learn object-identity based embeddings, which should represent what is distinctive about each object type compared to all the other object types in the same category. For example in the chair category we want the network to be able to tell apart lounge chairs and desk chairs.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Pose-invariant recognition and retrieval is an important problem in computer vision, and it has practical applications like robotic automation, automatic checkout systems, and inventory management. Many objects that belong to the same general category can look very different from different viewpoints, but humans have no difficulty recognizing them from any viewpoint. In pose-invariant recognition and retrieval the focus is on mapping object images to embedding vectors so that the embeddings of objects in the same category are pulled together for all the viewpoints we have, relative to the embeddings of objects from different categories.

Our work shows that the performance of this kind of pose-invariant learning can be improved significantly if the category-based learning is disentangled from the object-identity-based learning.

Fig. 1 shows what we mean by disentangling the category-based representation from the object-identity-based representation. Say an object database has images of different types of chairs and different types of stools. We want the network to learn category-based embedding vectors for the chair class and for the stool class. These embeddings need to capture what discriminates the chairs from the stools the most, which is whether there is a back-rest or not. At the same time we also want the network to learn object-identity based embeddings, which should represent what is distinctive about each object type compared to all the other object types in the same category. For example in the chair category we want the network to be able to tell apart lounge chairs and desk chairs.

Prior work has used multi-view deep networks to learn aggregated multi-view representations that capture the variability in how objects look under different pose transformations. These methods do well in category-level tasks when multiple views of the objects are available at inference time, but their performance gets worse when there is only a single view. Since real-world applications often need inference from single views, Ho et al. proposed a family of pose-invariant embeddings for recognition and retrieval, with constraints so that the single-view embeddings of an object are clustered around its multi-view embeddings, and those are clustered around a proxy embedding for the high-level category that the object belongs to. But this approach does not do a good enough job of separating the embeddings for two different objects in the same category (for example two different types of chairs, or two different kettles). So prior approaches perform well on category-level tasks but not on object-level tasks, which we show later in the experimental results (see Tables 2, 3).

The most significant difference between the previous methods and our method is this. Instead of learning representations that capture both category-specific and object-specific discriminative features in the same embedding space, we learn them at the same time in two distinct embedding spaces, as shown in the lower panel of Fig. 1. In the space for category-based representations, objects from the same category can be embedded close together, capturing what they share, while in the other space, for object identity-based representations, embeddings for different object types (in the same category or not) can be as separated as the attributes that differentiate them dictate. This lets our network learn object representations that are more discriminative overall, and this explains why our framework does better in both recognition and retrieval, especially in the harder case where only a single-viewpoint query image is available. For single-view object recognition we get an accuracy improvement of 20.0% on ModelNet40, 46.5% on FG3D, and 2.0% on ObjectPI. For single-view object retrieval we get a significant mAP improvement of 33.7% on ModelNet-40, 56.9% on FG3D, and 18.8% on ObjectPI.

To learn the dual embeddings at the same time we propose an encoder called the Pose-invariant Attention Network (PAN). PAN uses a shared CNN backbone to capture visual features that are common to both the category and the object-identity based representations, from a set of images of an object taken from different viewpoints. Then two fully connected layers map the visual features to separate low-dimensional category and object-identity based embeddings. PAN also uses self-attention to aggregate the visual features of objects from different views, which gives what we call multi-view embeddings. The dual embeddings, which are defined in Section 3, can be used for both category and object-level recognition and retrieval from single and multiple views.

To train the network we propose two pose-invariant losses, a category based one and an object-identity based one, and they are jointly optimized to learn the dual embeddings. The pose-invariant category loss clusters together instances of different objects that belong to the same category and separates instances from different categories in the category embedding space. The pose-invariant object-identity based loss clusters together instances with the same object-identity label and separates object instances that would otherwise be confused with each other, with two different object-identity labels from the same category, in the object embedding space.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Pose-invariant recognition and retrieval [1] is an important problem in computer vision with practical applications in robotic automation, automatic checkout systems, and inventory management. The appearance of many objects belonging to the same general category can vary a lot from different viewpoints, and yet humans have no difficulty recognizing them from arbitrary viewpoints. In pose-invariant recognition and retrieval, the focus is on mapping object images to embedding vectors such that the embeddings for objects belonging to the same category are pulled together for all available viewpoints, in relation to the embeddings for objects of different categories.

Our work demonstrates that the performance of pose-invariant learning as described above can be significantly improved if we disentangle the category-based learning from the object-identity-based learning.

Fig. 1 illustrates what we mean by disentangling the category-based representation from the object-identity-based representation. Assume that an object database contains images of different types of chairs and different types of stools. We would want our network to learn category-based embedding vectors for the chair class and for the stool class. These embeddings need to capture what is maximally discriminating between the chairs and the stools — the presence or absence of a back-rest. At the same time, we would want the network to learn object-identity based embeddings, which should represent what is distinctive about each object type relative to all other object types in the same category. For example, in the chair category, we would want the network to be able to discriminate between lounge chairs and desk chairs.

Prior work [2,3,4,5] has employed multi-view deep networks to learn aggregated multi-view representations capturing the variability in object appearance under different pose transformations. While these methods perform well in category-level tasks when multiple views of objects are available during inference, their performance degrades when only a single view is available. Since real-world applications often require inference from single views, Ho et al. [1] proposed a family of pose-invariant embeddings for both recognition and retrieval by imposing constraints such that the single-view embeddings of an object are clustered around its multi-view embeddings, which are in turn clustered around a proxy embedding representing the high-level category the object belongs to. However, this approach does not do a good enough job of separating the embeddings for two different objects of the same category (e.g., two different types of chairs, two different types of kettles). As a result, prior approaches perform well on category-level tasks but not on object-level tasks, as we demonstrate later in our experimental results (see Tables 2, 3).

Here is the most significant difference between the previous methods and the one proposed in this paper: rather than learning representations that capture both category-specific and object-specific discriminative features within the same embedding space, we learn them simultaneously in two distinct embedding spaces, as depicted in the lower panel of Fig. 1. In the space devoted to category-based representations, objects from the same category can be closely embedded together, capturing their shared characteristics, while in the space for object identity-based representations, embeddings for different object types (within the same category or otherwise) are allowed to be as separated as the attributes that differentiate them dictate. This strategy enables our network to learn object representations that are more discriminative overall, which explains the superior performance of our framework in both recognition and retrieval, especially in the more difficult case when only a single-viewpoint query image is available. For single-view object recognition, we get an improvement in accuracy of 20.0% on ModelNet40, 46.5% on FG3D, and 2.0% on ObjectPI. Similarly, for single-view object retrieval, we achieve a significant mAP improvement of 33.7% on ModelNet-40, 56.9% on FG3D, and 18.8% on ObjectPI.

In order to learn the dual embeddings simultaneously, we propose an encoder we call the Pose-invariant Attention Network (PAN). PAN uses a shared CNN backbone to capture visual features common to both the category and the object-identity based representations from a set of images of an object recorded from different viewpoints. The visual features are then mapped to separate low-dimensional category and object-identity based embeddings using two fully connected layers. PAN also aggregates the visual features of objects from different views using self-attention to generate what we call multi-view embeddings. The dual embeddings, defined in Section 3, can be used for both category and object-level recognition and retrieval from single and multiple views.

For training the network, we propose two pose-invariant losses, category-based and object-identity based, that are jointly optimized to learn the dual embeddings. The pose-invariant category loss clusters together instances of different objects belonging to the same category while separating instances from different categories in the category embedding space. The pose-invariant object-identity based loss, on the other hand, clusters together instances carrying the same object-identity label and separates otherwise mutually confusing object instances with different object-identity labels from the same category in the object embedding space.

References:
[1] Chih-Hui Ho, Pedro Morgado, Amir Persekian, and Nuno Vasconcelos. Pies: Pose invariant embeddings. In Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) , 2019.
[2] Hang Su, Subhransu Maji, Evangelos Kalogerakis, and Erik G. Learned-Miller. Multi-view convolutional neural networks for 3d shape recognition. In International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) , 2015.
[3] Asako Kanezaki, Yasuyuki Matsushita, and Yoshifumi Nishida. Rotationnet: Joint object categorization and pose estimation using multiviews from unsupervised viewpoints. Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) , pages 5010–5019, 2018.
[4] Xinwei He, Yang Zhou, Zhichao Zhou, Song Bai, and Xiang Bai. Triplet-center loss for multi-view 3d object retrieval. Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) , 2018.
[5] Zhirong Wu, S. Song, A. Khosla, Fisher Yu, Linguang Zhang, Xiaoou Tang, and J. Xiao. 3d shapenets: A deep representation for volumetric shapes. In Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) , pages 1912–1920, Los Alamitos, CA, USA, 2015. IEEE Computer Society.
